newsitem.title: UK: Cocoa slumps in bear raid, base metals shine.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa slumps in bear raid, base metals shine.

text.p: Cocoa prices took a tumble on Wednesday as the market succumbed to a "bear" raid while, in other commodities, base metals regained some shine on an influx of fund buying.

London bellwether May cocoa futures lost some five percent in value on the day, closing a sharp 45 pounds sterling down at 879 sterling, mainly due to trade selling, although a daily dose of producer selling persisted.

Traders said New York's equivalent cocoa market started the sell-off on Tuesday night, and this dragged the sterling-denominated London market lower. A stronger pound sterling against the French franc was also psychologically bearish.
"I think it's liquidation of longs and disappointment by the lack of follow through, and a bit of a bear raid," said one trader.
In base metals, copper extended its recent gains, going above $2,230 per tonne on the London Metal Exchange as New York's Comex opened firmer.
Premiums for prompt delivery also widened, implying tight supply, and shortcovering also helped to lift the market.
Three months delivery ended at $2,240 a tonne for a $36 gain.
Nickel and zinc also stole the limelight, with zinc hitting fresh two-year highs at $1,190 before closing at $1,184, up $15, while nickel touched a fresh 7-1/2 month peak at around $7,825.
Traders said improving fundamentals and a constructive chart outlook together with an influx of fund money buying helped both zinc and nickel.
An analyst at CRU International told an industry meeting in New York on Wednesday that the zinc supply/demand balance would remain in deficit for at least two years.
Gold fixed $3.35 lower at $342.95 an ounce and just above the morning fix which was a fresh low since September 14, 1993 of $342.05.
"It is still under pressure. The sentiment is still bearish and the overall downtrend is still intact," said one dealer.
"The very strong dollar isn't helping gold either," he added.
More pressingly, the bullion market was still uncomfortable about the possibility of central bank selling. Last Thursday's heavy sales were immediately interpreted as the work of central banks.
White sugar burst higher on trade buying on the back of an unusually heavy volume of business.
The surge in London was sparked by technical strength in New York.
Coffee's recent rally seemed stalled on Wednesday, with growing losses in New York taking London prices even lower on profit-taking after a slow morning trade.
Soybean prices on the Chicago Board of Trade were lower early on recent rains in South America which were deemed conducive for the crop.
